full_judgment:
5. It is submitted by the petitioner that she purchased the case land on 26-10-1964 and it was long after 20 years that the respondents filed the Revision Case before the ADC (Rev). Khulna under section 53 of the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913, It is submitted that the member of the Land Appeal Board failed to consider that a person without availing the remedy by way as provided in sections 22, 23 of the Public Demands Recovery Act within the time limit a party has no right to seek revision under section 53 of the Public Demands Recovery Act. The petitioner purchased the land in good faith in auction for establishing dairy and agriculture farm. The Member of the Land Appeal Board did not consider that in CS and SA records the land was recorded in the names of the former owners, and they having permanent right it was never recorded in the name of the Government nor it was a public easement property. It was a private property being permanent private tenancy. It is further submitted that a revisional application under section 53 of the Public Demands Recovery Act can only be filed on question of law and new question of fact cannot be raised for the first time. 

 6. An affidavit-in-opposition has been filed by the respondent Nos. 10 and 14 contending, inter alia, that the lands shown to have been sold in auction were beds of rivers and khal at the relevant time. These have been in use by the local public from time immemorial. The lands are public easement. These lands ought to have been recorded in government Khas Khatian No. 1 as non-retainable khas land of private landlords within the ambit of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Due to either inadvertence of settlement officials or fraud of the private landlords Nripendra Nath Ghosh and others, the lands were recorded in their names most illegally. Taking advantage of such illegal omission and the absence of the private landlords Mr. ATM Nurul Islam, husband of the petitioner, who was posted at Dumuria as the Engineer, Public Health Department at the relevant time, "brought to bear unholy influence on the local Revenue Officer of Dumuria and got the land sold in auction in a certificate case beyond the knowledge of the public at large by suppression of notices and proclamations". He purchased the land in the name of his wife and after obtaining certified copies, managed to make the records of the Certificate Case disappear with a view to concealing fraud and forgery. The petitioner got her name mutated in the SA Khatian beyond the knowledge of the public and abstained from payment of rent to conceal her auction purchase from the local public and the petitioner preferred an appeal against the impugned judgment and order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Khulna and others and also filed Title Suit No. 181 of 1986 on 29-5-86 in the 1st Court of Munsif which on transfer to the court of Additional Assistant Judge, Khulna, was renumbered as Title Suit No. 96 of 1990 for declaration that the order of Additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue setting aside the auction sale (Annexure-C) in this writ petition was void, illegal and for permanent injunction. The suit was dismissed on contest by judgment and decree dated 27-3-90 and 3-4-1990 respectively with the findings, inter alia, that the suit land were river and canals, that some of the plaintiffs were minor at the time of alleged auction purchase and the auction sale was in contravention of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 and the plaintiff (petitioner in this writ petition) failed to prove her title or auction purchase and possession of the suit land. Certified copy of the Judgment and Decree is annexed to the-affidavit-in- opposition and marked as Annexure-1 and 2 respectively. The petitioner preferred Title Appeal No. 88 of 1990 against the said judgment and decree but the appellate Court was pleased to allow withdrawal of the application of the petitioner by order No. 21 dated 16-6-93. Certified copy of the memorandum of appeal and withdrawal order are annexed to the affidavit-in-opposition and marked as Annexure 3 and 3(a) respectively. 

 13. It appears from the judgment that there is admission by the lawyer appearing for the petitioner that some of the lands sold in question were originally public easement and that their nature and character changed after sale by auction. It is therefore clear that the ADC (Rev) Khulna found that at the time of the auction sale the properties in question were public easement. The Additional Commissioner who by his judgment dated 31-8-86 (Annexure-D) allowed the appeal of the petitioner but did not come to any finding as to the nature of the properties sold in the auction. He did not disagree with the finding of the Additional Deputy Commissioner that the properties were public easement. It appears that the Additional Commissioner allowed the appeal on the ground that there was inordinate delay in filing the application under section 53 of the Public Demands Recovery Act to set aside the auction sale. The Additional Commissioner raised a question why the petitioners did not raise their voice for 20 years. As there was no explanation for this inordinate delay it weakened the revisional application. He therefore held that it was not reasonable now to cancel a title established about 20 years back. The belated plea of public easement was unacceptable. The Additional Commissioner further held that the respondent did not deposit the money which is to be paid back to the auction purchaser in the event of the sale being set aside. He further held that the respondent's prayer for setting aside the sale should have been filed initially before the certificate officer who held the auction as provided under section 23 of the PDR Act. The Member Land Administration Board by Annexure E allowed the appeal by the respondents against the judgment and order dated 31-8-86 passed by the Additional Commissioner. The Member Land Administration Board after examining the record, inter alia, found that plot No.139 comprising 11.85 acres was a river and 49 other plots comprising 59.40 acres were khal. He therefore held that river and khal are for the use of public easement and this is recognized by all. Further, under section 20(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 rivers and khal could not be retained by tenants under section 2 of the said Act, Therefore, the sale by auction of river and khal by the certificate officer in Certificate case No. H7650/61-62 was found to be illegal. We find from the aforementioned judgments of 3 Revenue Authorities that the land sold by auction to the present petitioner comprised of river and khal. The respondent in their supplementary affidavit-in-opposition have annexed certified copies of CS Kh No. 2 which was sold by auction of the petitioner. Although Annexure 4 shows the predecessor of the petitioner to be recorded as tenants by the land in question have been described as (নদী ও খাল)  (River and Khal). It is also mentioned against these plots সাধারনের ব্যবহার" plots No. 139 and 671 have been described as নদী প্রকাশ্য খাল নগর নদী সাধারনের ব্যবাহার্য্য Annexure 5 to the affidavit which is certified copy of the CS Map prepared by the Government in 1922-23 in respect of Mowza Balabunia No. 127, Sheet No. 2 covering the disputed lands clearly shows that the lands sold constitute the bed of some rivers and navigable canals. These documents were placed before the Land Administration Board which as we have seen found that the properties in question comprising of river and khal. In the case of Mohammad Gani vs Deputy Commissioner, Faridpur reported in 15 DLR 112 a Division Bench of the High Court at Dhaka held that navigation-right over rivers and waterways, cannot be interfered with (except provided otherwise by specific provisions of law) by the Government. Such right with other incidental rights are universally recognized as vested in public. Justice SM Murshed, as he then was, delivering the judgment in that case further observed; 

 14. We have already seen that the properties in question being river and khal could not be retained by the recorded tenants under section 20(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Therefore it was rightly held by the Member Land Administration Board that the properties in question could not be recorded in the name of Nripendra Nath Ghosh and others after the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force in 1950.
